newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian corporate law reform announcement Wed.
newsitem.headline: Australian corporate law reform announcement Wed.

text.p: The first announcement to come out of the Australian government's Corporate Law Economic Reform Program (CLER) will be made on Wednesday and the first reform proposal may be published as early as next month.
That is according to the man responsible for implementing the three-month-old reform process, Senator Ian Campbell.
In an interview with Reuters this week, Campbell said:
- he will be naming the members of the government's new Business Regulation Advisory Group on Wednesday;
- the policy paper to be published in July will deal with reform of Australian accounting standards; and
- the program generally was running on schedule to meet its 1998 deadline for legislative enactment of the reform package.
Campbell also said the government was looking at a number of major reforms including:
- a new broadly based peak council with general oversight responsibility for the Australian Accounting Standards Board;
- a significant reduction in the $A500,000 threshold for the "professional investor" fundraising exemption; and
- new criteria for the mezzanine financing exemption to replace the existing focus on the number of offers made.
Campbell said the final outcome was likely to be "the most significant reform of corporations law in Australia ever".

"If we get financial reporting right, fundraising right, takeovers right, and you combine that with Wallis, and all of that gets implemented over the next 18 months, it is a big hit," Campbell said. "It is huge. It will be the most significant reform of corporations law in Australia ever, I suspect.
"...We say 'There are barriers to growth and we are going to knock them over. We are going to make it easier to do business,'" Campbell said.

The CLER programme was launched by Treasurer Peter Costello on March 4 with the stated intention "to improve Australia's corporate law as part of the Coalition Government's drive to promote business and economic development".
Costello said at the time that the corporations law was "too prescriptive, legalistic and out of touch with modern commercial practices".
He said the Government would also address "as a matter of priority" the reform of Australian accounting standards.
The first stage of the programme involved round-table discussions with interested parties and is now almost complete, Campbell said this week.

The "key" policy areas under scrutiny have been fundraising, takeovers, futures and securities markets, directors' duties and electronic commerce; as well as the reform of Australian accounting standards.
Campbell said the second stage of the Program, which was already underway, will involve drafting detailed reform proposals covering each of those areas.
There will then be an opportunity for more public consultation before legislative amendments are drafted.
"We are publishing a policy (on reform of Australian accounting standards) in July," Campbell said.
"That will set out the government's policy on the reform of the Australian Accounting Standards Board.
"In terms of the reform of the Corporations Law, a policy will be published in about August and again it will say this is what the Government is proposing to do," he said.
"It will not be a discussion paper. It will be the Government saying we have heard what everyone said and this is what we are going to do," Campbell said.
"(The reforms) are all judgment calls," he said.

"You are never going to please everybody but ultimately you have got to make decisions about which way you are going to go and we've made it clear our decisions will be based on what's best for the Australian economy, what's best for creating jobs, what's best for building enterprises and, of course, maintaining investor protection which we see as important as all those other objectives," Campbell said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
